introduction: These are government actions that pursued a benefit for the public as a whole while placing a material cost on a smaller, existing trade or group. For a state or local action, the relevant public is that jurisdiction's community. The burden can be lost work, an ended product or harvest market, a forced change in established operations, or another material livelihood effect; it need not be a proven layoff or the complete end of a person's career. This is a substantial starting point, not a claim to have found every such event.

Every item below clears that event-level screen. The plain-language explanation comes first, followed by its screening disposition and the more detailed record. Later work can measure a particular worksite or occupation group's losses, assess competing causes and prepare certification files. Inclusion here does not establish that every worker or firm in an industry was harmed, and this document does not advocate for particular people.

The list is open. An unlisted action or affected group may qualify under the same rule, regardless of industry, jurisdiction, period, or resemblance to these examples. A person can lose a principal job and suffer a material loss while still holding another job. A petition must be decided by the rule and its evidence, never by whether the event already appears in this register.

Stable IDs preserve links to the evidence spreadsheet; missing numbers reflect research leads that did not clear this screen. The salmon seasons are separate government actions. The citation audit distinguishes reopened anchors, corrected links and sources whose direct text still requires verification; a source check does not prove a particular worksite loss.

The event screen and Cornerstone eligibility rule remain unchanged. Section 4 of the Fourteenth Amendment separately prohibits the United States and every state from paying any claim for the loss or emancipation of an enslaved person, and declares such claims illegal and void. That constitutional limit resolves a claim for compensation arising from emancipation regardless of the former owner's loyalty or state of residence; no additional Cornerstone exclusion is needed.

An official GAO inventory of 73 named major 1988–1995 BRAC sites with estimated civilian job losses is represented with exact decision rounds. The register names 18 of 23 major installations actually closed in the 2005 round where a baseline workforce projection or other group record supports a material effect; the other five need further causation review. Some smaller and separately authorized closures are also included, but their universe is not enumerated. GAO found no aggregate count adequate to measure the business and household effects of eminent-domain redevelopment. Many other jurisdiction and period inventories remain open.

The continuous register has 231 qualifying event-level entries after six supplemental sweeps. Every retained row has a plain-language rule explanation and at least one linked source, but the independent holdout found additional obvious historical examples. It is a substantial open starting point, not an estimated majority or a closed category list. The principal remaining research is a bounded inventory of smaller BRAC actions, seasonal fishery orders, state/local bans, public project takings and site-level affected groups, with separate accounting for competing causes and past compensation.
Coverage sources.  GAO major BRAC sites and job estimates; GAO on eminent-domain data limits.

Keep this register open to newly identified actions and affected groups under the same material-effect rule. For a future coverage percentage, define a counting unit and a bounded jurisdiction and period; enumerate official action inventories, deduplicate, and independently check omissions. Group and worksite evidence must also separate the government's action from competing causes, transfers, redevelopment work and existing compensation.

events.title: 2005 BRAC closure of Marine Corps Support Activity Kansas City
events.instrument: 2005 Defense Base Closure and Realignment action
events.action: The federal BRAC decision closed the Kansas City Marine Corps Support Activity in a nationwide effort to use defense resources efficiently; the Navy confirms its operational closure in September 2011.
events.why: The federal government closed this defense support activity to advance military efficiency, materially removing the established work of its civilian and contractor staff at that site.

events.title: 2004 congressional closure of Naval Station Roosevelt Roads
events.sovereign: United States / Congress and Department of the Navy
events.instrument: Section 8132, fiscal 2004 Defense Appropriations Act
events.action: Congress directed closure of the naval station following the end of training on Vieques, and the Navy closed it in March 2004 as a military infrastructure decision.

events.title: 2015 closure of the primary directed Pacific sardine fishery
events.instrument: Pacific sardine annual specification and harvest cutoff
events.action: Federal managers closed the primary directed Pacific sardine fishery off Washington, Oregon and California when biomass fell below the conservation cutoff.
events.why: The federal conservation rule closed a formerly productive directed sardine fishery, materially removing that source of income for its existing fleet and processors.
events.group_record: Existing purse-seine vessels, crews and sardine processors lost the primary directed catch. California's official request reported a 90% lower statewide sardine ex-vessel value in 2015 than its 2010–14 average.
events.causation: The natural biomass fall is a strong competing cause; live-bait, minor directed and incidental catch remained legal and some vessels switched species. Do not label total revenue decline as caused only by the closure.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: NOAA identifies the initial 2015–16 closure; California's request reports ex-vessel impact and exceptions. Natural depletion and government restriction must be separated.
events.further: Compare vessel-level past sardine revenue and gear permits to subsequent catch, other species, processing activity and disaster aid.

events.title: 2021 Upper Cook Inlet East Side setnet restrictions

events.title: 2016 FDA consumer antibacterial-wash ingredient rule
events.sovereign: United States / Food and Drug Administration
events.instrument: Consumer Antiseptic Wash Final Rule, 81 FR 61106
events.action: FDA determined 19 active ingredients, including triclosan and triclocarban, could no longer be marketed without drug approval in ordinary consumer antiseptic washes to protect public health.
events.why: FDA restricted an established antibacterial-wash market for health reasons, imposing material product-line and reformulation costs on the firms that supplied it.
events.group_record: Affected wash makers, ingredient suppliers and private-label firms had to reformulate, relabel, obtain approvals or withdraw products. FDA modeled 2,093 affected product codes, one-time relabeling costs of $18.9–$53.4 million and potentially substantial reformulation costs.
events.causation: Some companies anticipated the rule and voluntarily changed formulas; replacement soaps can preserve sales and work. The model is not a realized net-income or job-loss total.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: FDA final rule and its impact analysis establish the legal market change, product count and estimated compliance costs; realization varies by firm.
events.further: Identify the affected SKUs and ingredient suppliers and compare actual conversion, discontinued lines and cost against pre-rule baselines.

events.title: 2019 FDA consumer antiseptic-rub ingredient rule
events.sovereign: United States / Food and Drug Administration
events.instrument: Consumer Antiseptic Rub Final Rule, 84 FR 14847
events.action: FDA made 28 active ingredients in nonprescription consumer antiseptic rubs ineligible for marketing through the OTC monograph, requiring drug approval or a change to the affected sanitizer and wipe products.
events.why: The federal health rule removed a defined set of formerly marketed sanitizer ingredients and imposed material product changes on the firms using them.
events.group_record: Existing makers of the covered products had to reformulate, relabel or discontinue them. FDA modeled about $1.07–$2.50 million in aggregate one-time reformulation and labeling costs for the affected product cohort.
events.causation: Ethyl alcohol, isopropyl alcohol and benzalkonium chloride were deferred and were not banned by this rule. The impact model is prospective; alternatives and other product lines limit net harm.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: FDA guidance identifies the final monograph decision; FDA impact analysis identifies affected products and modeled costs while excluding deferred common ingredients.
events.further: Match actual product lists and ingredient use to the covered 28 ingredients, then verify realized costs and displaced sales.

events.title: 2024 FDA brominated-vegetable-oil food-use revocation
events.sovereign: United States / Food and Drug Administration
events.instrument: Final rule revoking 21 CFR 180.30, 89 FR 55040
events.action: FDA revoked permission to use brominated vegetable oil as a stabilizer in food after concluding the available evidence no longer supported its safety.
events.why: FDA ended a previously lawful food-ingredient use for public health, directly forcing the remaining small group of user firms to replace formulas and labels at material cost.
events.group_record: A small cohort of beverage and flavor-concentrate makers still used BVO. FDA's analysis found eight parent companies with confirmed use in 2021 and modeled $6.6–$16.4 million in first-year industry reformulation and relabeling costs, much of which could be passed on.
events.causation: Most large beverage makers had already switched voluntarily; FDA expected low incremental long-run costs and replacement formulas. Model costs cannot be assumed to be job losses or a material net loss for each firm.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: FDA confirms the final revocation and timing; its final impact analysis estimates eight confirmed user companies in 2021 and a modeled first-year cost range, not actual layoffs.
events.further: Verify affected 2024–25 products, actual formula and label expenditure, cost pass-through and discontinued lines for the remaining users.

events.title: 2019 California retail pet-store sourcing ban
events.instrument: AB 485, 2017 Statutes chapter 740
events.action: California required retail shops selling dogs, cats or rabbits to source them from shelters and rescue groups, ending ordinary breeder-sourced store sales to reduce puppy-mill harm.
events.why: California pursued animal welfare by ending breeder-sourced pet sales in existing stores, materially restricting the stores and suppliers that depended on that trade.
events.group_record: Pet stores that had relied on breeder-sourced animals and their suppliers lost that lawful retail channel; 2020 legislation later closed a remaining loophole. Store workers' overall job outcome requires store-level evidence.
events.causation: Shelter/rescue placements, other pet products, direct breeder sales and a later amendment may offset or alter each business's material loss; do not assume every pet store was affected.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: The chaptered 2017 statute and Governor's later summary establish the 2019 breeder-source restriction and 2020 tightening; impact by store remains to verify.
events.further: Match pre-2019 retail sales and supplier contracts to post-law activity and identify shops with a materially lost animal-sales line.

events.title: 2020 Maryland retail dog and cat sale ban
events.instrument: No More Puppy- and Kitten-Mills Act of 2018, chapter 237
events.action: Maryland prohibited retail pet stores from selling or otherwise transferring dogs and cats to address puppy- and kitten-mill harms, after a delayed implementation period.

events.causation: Direct sales from breeders and shelter displays may continue; some stores did not sell covered animals and pet supplies remain. Actual firm and worker losses require transaction records.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: Enacted law gives the restriction and delayed date; legislative fiscal note describes lost retail sales and breeder channels without proving a specific store closure.

events.title: 2024 New York pet-store sale ban
events.instrument: Puppy Mill Pipeline Act, chapter 681 of 2022

events.instrument: Local Law 142 of 2013 and DSNY implementation

events.title: Garrison Dam flooding of Fort Berthold land
events.sovereign: United States / Army Corps of Engineers
events.instrument: Pick–Sloan / Flood Control Act of 1944
events.action: The United States built Garrison Dam for regional flood control, power and other public purposes, filling Lake Sakakawea on the Missouri River.
events.why: A federal dam built for broad flood-control and power benefits flooded established Fort Berthold homes and working land, materially burdening a concentrated community.
events.group_record: GAO records 152,360 acres flooded on the Fort Berthold Reservation; Interior had estimated 289 families in the flood area. Homes, ranches and all of the reservation's irrigable land were affected.
events.causation: Prior land payments and later tribal settlements must be credited; the report's acreage is a reservation-level aggregate, not a roster of uncompensated individuals. Separate crops, housing, timber and businesses by parcel.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: GAO Table 1 quantifies reservation flood acreage and family exposure; the Corps confirms project and public purposes.

events.title: 1942 wartime exclusion and incarceration of Japanese Americans
events.instrument: Executive Order 9066 and civilian exclusion orders
events.action: The federal government asserted a nationwide wartime-defense purpose, designated military areas and forcibly removed and incarcerated Japanese Americans from the West Coast.
events.why: Federal exclusion orders asserted national defense while imposing devastating material loss on a smaller American group; later Congress rejected the premise and provided redress, which must be counted.
events.group_record: More than 120,000 people were uprooted; many lost homes, property, businesses and work. The displaced cohort included U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents.
events.causation: Congress later recognized the action as a grave injustice rooted in racial prejudice and war hysteria, not a valid military necessity. The 1948 property-claims law and 1988 redress payments must be credited; this record does not suggest any additional individual entitlement.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: NPS documents the order and 120,000-plus forced removals; National Archives explains the later congressional apology and $20,000 redress. Stated national-security purpose is expressly described as a claim later repudiated.
events.further: Match business and work loss categories to contemporaneous records and the two redress programs, without relitigating the event's wrongful character.

events.title: 1942 Oak Ridge Manhattan Project land acquisition
events.sovereign: United States / Army Corps of Engineers
events.instrument: Manhattan Project Oak Ridge site acquisition
events.action: The Army acquired and fenced 56,000 acres for a secret wartime uranium-enrichment center serving national defense.
events.why: A national-defense project took established rural land and work in one local area, imposing concentrated material costs.
events.group_record: National Park Service records identify longstanding rural communities whose homes, land and livelihoods were displaced by the site's acquisition.
events.causation: Original purchase or condemnation payments, temporary wartime jobs and later land use may offset different households differently; acreage is site size, not a count of uncompensated farms.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: NPS identifies displaced established communities and livelihoods; DOE documents the 1942–43 acquisition and 56,000-acre security perimeter.
events.further: Review federal land-acquisition files and community records for affected farms, shops and compensation.

events.title: 1942 Los Alamos Manhattan Project land acquisition
events.sovereign: United States / Army Corps of Engineers
events.instrument: Manhattan Project Los Alamos laboratory site acquisition
events.action: The Army acquired the Pajarito Plateau for the wartime weapons laboratory, removing homesteaders and closing the Los Alamos Ranch School.
events.why: A federal wartime laboratory displaced an established small homesteading and school community to serve national defense.
events.group_record: NPS records identify local Hispanic and other homesteaders who abandoned cabins and farm use; 12 homesteads remained with original owners and seven with their families at acquisition, while the established ranch school closed.
events.causation: Some residents later worked at the laboratory. Tribal cultural and land interests are distinct from a homestead owner's loss; property and school settlements must be credited.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: NPS documents homesteader and school removal and a 19-homestead original/family ownership subset, not total displaced individuals.
events.further: Match the 1942 acquisition files to homesteads, seasonal farm uses, ranch school business and later work.

events.title: 1943 Hanford Manhattan Project land requisition
events.sovereign: United States / Army Corps of Engineers
events.instrument: Manhattan Project Hanford site land requisition
events.action: The United States took Columbia River land for the Hanford plutonium-production project, ordering residents out on short notice for wartime defense work.
events.why: A national-defense land requisition removed established farms, homes and businesses in one local area for a wider wartime project.
events.group_record: NPS reports roughly 1,500 residents in White Bluffs, Hanford, Richland and nearby communities affected, including farmers and local enterprises; some owners had 30–90 days to leave.
events.causation: Initial settlements, wartime replacement work and Native land and use interests differ by group; the 1,500 is a population estimate, not a job-loss or unpaid-claim count.
events.disposition: Qualifying event; precise worksite and group effects remain to be measured
events.citation_check: NPS identifies communities, approximate resident group and short notice; site-specific compensation must be reconciled.
events.further: Review requisition, farm and business records and original settlements; separate tribal use interests from private holdings.
